review.name: Ratification of the U.S. Constitution
review.lo: LO 1.5.A — Explain the impact of political negotiation and compromise at the Constitutional Convention on the development of the constitutional system.
review.core: The Constitution was bargained into existence. Several of those bargains resolved a dispute for the moment without settling the underlying question, which is why some of them still generate argument.
blocks: The Virginia Plan proposed a bicameral legislature with representation in both chambers based on population, favoring large states. The New Jersey Plan proposed a single chamber with equal representation for every state, favoring small states.

Great (Connecticut) Compromise — bicameral Congress, House by population, Senate equal by state · Electoral College — electors chosen by each state select the president, rather than Congress or a direct popular vote · Three-Fifths Compromise — a formula counting a state’s enslaved population for representation in the House and for taxation · Postponing until 1808 a decision on banning the importation of enslaved persons · Agreement to add a Bill of Rights to address Anti-Federalist concerns
Proposal: a two-thirds vote in both houses of Congress, or a convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures. Ratification: three-fourths of the states. The president has no formal role.

The debate over the role of the national government, the powers of the states, and the rights of individuals remains at the center of constitutional argument — visible in disputes over government surveillance after the September 11 attacks and over the role of government in public school education.
traps: Treating a compromise as a solution
Several compromises worked by postponing or papering over a conflict. Saying what a compromise settled is only half the answer; say what it left open.
Two-thirds proposes. Three-fourths ratifies. These are separate stages, and questions are built around the confusion.
